484.title: A mercy to the worlds
484.hook: We sent you only as a mercy to all the worlds (21:107)
484.carry: the dog at the well counts
484.howItsDone: Muslims often quote 21:107 when describing the Prophet's character, and stories of his kindness to animals, like the man who gave water to a dog, are often taught to children.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Zakariyya, who asked in secret not to be left alone. Your line was don't leave me alone.

For most of this surah, the prophets pass by one at a time. Ibrahim in the fire. Lut. Nuh. Dawud and Sulayman. Ayyub, Yunus, Zakariyya, Maryam. The surah is named for them: Al-Anbiya, the Prophets. Then, near the end, the camera turns. It looks straight at the one hearing the surah first, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and sums up his whole mission in one line.

Verse one hundred seven. Pickthall: "We sent thee not save as a mercy for the peoples." In Arabic, rahmatan lil-'alamin: a mercy for the worlds. That last word, 'alamin, is the one from the Qur'an's very first page: praise belongs to God, Lord of the 'alamin, Lord of the Worlds. Pickthall translates it peoples here, and worlds there. Both are fair. Some commentators say it reaches past people: humans, jinn, animals, everything that is. And notice the shape: not save as, only as. The verse doesn't call mercy one part of his mission among others. It says he was sent only as mercy. There's a hadith in Muslim's collection. Once, he was asked to curse the idolaters who opposed him. He said he was not sent to curse; he was sent as a mercy. And the mercy keeps reaching past people. Bukhari records his story of a man, desperately thirsty himself, who climbed down into a well, filled his shoe with water and gave it to a dog panting at the edge, and God forgave him. The companions asked, is there reward even for animals? He said, in every living, breathing thing there is reward. So a mercy to the worlds isn't only a title. It sets a standard for anyone who follows him: the dog at the well counts. The ant counts. The stranger counts.
screen: `NOT SAVE AS A MERCY.` · `'ALAMIN: THE SAME WORD AS PAGE ONE.` · `NOT SENT TO CURSE.` · `WATER FOR A DOG AT THE WELL.`

segments.voice: Look around your day for one living thing you could ease: a plant that needs water, a bird that would take a dish of it, a pet that wants your attention, a person who's been short with you. Choose one, and picture easing it, slowly, in detail. If you pray, you can ask to be a little more like the one sent as a mercy.
Rahmatan lil-'alamin. A mercy to the worlds: the Prophet's whole mission in one line, reaching people, animals and everything that is.
Your line: the dog at the well counts. Mercy reaches every living, breathing thing. Until tomorrow.

485.title: Proclaim the pilgrimage
485.hook: Ibrahim is told to call people to pilgrimage, and they come on foot and on lean camels from every deep valley (22:27)
485.howItsDone: Muslims who are physically and financially able make the Hajj to Mecca at least once in their lives, in the month of Dhul-Hijjah, repeating the talbiya, 'labbayk allahumma labbayk', as they travel.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rahmatan lil-'alamin, a mercy to the worlds. Your line was the dog at the well counts.

A valley with almost nothing in it. Rock, heat, and one small house of stone that an old man and his son have just finished building. No road leads here. No city. And the old man is told to stand and call all of humanity to come. Commentators report that Ibrahim asked the obvious question: my Lord, how will my voice reach them? And the answer, as they tell it, was: you call, and the reaching is up to Us. Today, a new surah, Al-Hajj, the Pilgrimage, and that call.
screen: `AN EMPTY VALLEY, ONE HOUSE OF STONE.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-seven. Pickthall: "And proclaim unto mankind the Pilgrimage. They will come unto thee on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep ravine". The verb for proclaim is adhdhin, from the same root as the adhan, the call to prayer, and as udhun, the ear. A call made out loud, meant to be heard. Then look who comes. On foot, first. Then on every lean camel; the word is damir, thin, worn down from the long road. The verse doesn't picture people arriving rested and polished. It pictures them tired. And from every fajj 'amiq, every deep mountain pass, the kind of narrow gap between hills a road squeezes through. The camels have changed. Pilgrims now come by plane and bus, from Jakarta and Lagos and Detroit. They come from every valley, still. On the way, pilgrims repeat the talbiya over and over: labbayk allahumma labbayk. Here I am, O God, here I am. Some commentators connect that line with this verse: an answer to a call made in an empty valley. Not everyone can go. The Qur'an makes Hajj a duty only for those able to make the journey. But the picture belongs to everyone: thin camels, tired feet, and a voice that somehow carried.
screen: `ADHDHIN: CALL SO EARS HEAR.` · `ON FOOT, ON LEAN CAMELS.` · `FROM EVERY DEEP MOUNTAIN PASS.` · `LABBAYK: HERE I AM.`

segments.voice: Picture one pilgrim coming down a mountain road on foot, then another from a desert, then a bus from a city you've never visited, a plane full of grandmothers, a young man who saved for ten years. Let the roads fill until you can't count them. If you pray, you can pray for the ones on the road right now.
Talbiya. The pilgrims' repeated call, here I am, O God, here I am, answering Ibrahim's call from an empty valley. Today's word.
Your line: they come from every valley. Far roads, one answer: here I am. Day four hundred eighty-five.

486.title: Neither flesh nor blood
486.hook: neither the meat nor the blood reaches Allah, but your mindfulness does (22:37)
486.howItsDone: Muslims who can afford it offer an animal at Eid al-Adha, often through a local farm, a mosque program or a charity abroad, and share the meat with family, neighbors and people in need.

segments.voice: Yesterday: talbiya, the pilgrims' answer to Ibrahim's call. Your line was they come from every valley.

On the morning of Eid al-Adha, in backyards, farms and licensed slaughterhouses around the world, families offer an animal: a sheep, a goat, a share in a cow or a camel. It's the festival of sacrifice, remembering Ibrahim's readiness to give up his son, and the ram given in his place. For a lot of people, it's the biggest meal of the year. And in the middle of the surah that sets out these rites, the Qur'an stops to say something that sounds almost like it's undercutting the whole thing.
screen: `A SHEEP, A GOAT, A SHARE IN A COW.`

segments.voice: Verse thirty-seven. Pickthall: "Their flesh and their blood reach not Allah, but the devotion from you reacheth Him." God doesn't need the meat, or the blood. The word Pickthall translates devotion is taqwa, which this path has met before: mindfulness of God, a careful awareness that shapes what you do. That's the only part that arrives. Commentators mention a pre-Islamic custom of smearing sacrificial blood on the Ka'ba's walls, and read this verse as quietly ending that idea: the blood was never the point. So where does the meat go? A verse just before says it: eat of it, and feed the one who is poor and content and the one who asks. Many scholars recommend dividing it in three, a third for the family, a third for friends and neighbors, a third for those in need, though they treat that split as good practice rather than a strict rule. The animal feeds people; the intention goes to God. And this reaches past Eid. The first hadith in Bukhari's collection says that actions are judged by intentions, and every person gets what they intended. Two people hand over the same envelope at a wedding. One gives to be seen giving; one gives because they love the couple. The envelopes weigh the same. Only one, in this verse's picture, reaches anywhere at all. The question isn't how big the gift is. It's what's traveling inside it.
screen: `FLESH AND BLOOD DON'T REACH GOD.` · `TAQWA IS WHAT ARRIVES.` · `THE MEAT FEEDS PEOPLE.` · `ACTIONS ARE BY INTENTIONS.`

segments.voice: Think of something you gave recently, or are about to give, money, time, a present, a favor, and ask gently, without judging the answer: who was it for? If part of it was for being thanked or seen, that's human; set the gift down again in your mind with one clean reason. If you pray, you can offer it to God.
Taqwa. Mindfulness of God, the only part of a sacrifice that reaches Him, not the flesh or the blood. Today's word.
Your line: only the heart reaches him. The meat feeds people; the intention travels on. See you tomorrow.

487.title: Blind hearts
487.hook: it is not the eyes that go blind but the hearts in the chests (22:46)
487.howItsDone: Muslim teachers often quote 22:46 when speaking about reflection, and the Qur'an's repeated call to travel and consider the ruins of past peoples is part of how many Muslims think about history.

segments.voice: Yesterday: taqwa, the only part of a sacrifice that reaches God. Your line was only the heart reaches him.

A caravan route in Arabia runs past ruins: a well nobody draws from, a tall, strong building with no one inside. Travelers pass them on the way north to Syria, water the camels nearby, maybe glance up. They've seen them a hundred times. They're scenery. Surah Al-Hajj points at exactly this kind of place, a town fallen in on its own roofs, a deserted well, a lofty tower, and then asks the travelers a question about their own eyes.

Verse forty-six begins with a question: haven't they traveled in the land, so that they might have hearts to understand with, and ears to hear with? Then the line this day is named for. Pickthall: "For indeed it is not the eyes that grow blind, but it is the hearts, which are within the bosoms, that grow blind." Their eyes worked perfectly. They saw the ruins. What didn't happen was understanding. The verse puts seeing somewhere other than the eyes: hearts to understand with. In the Qur'an, the heart, qalb, is where a person understands, decides and takes things in, not only where they feel. Some scholars connect the word with a root about turning; in that picture, the heart is the part of you that can turn. A hadith in Bukhari says there is a piece of flesh in the body: if it's sound, the whole body is sound, and if it's corrupt, the whole body is corrupt, and that piece is the heart. Notice the odd little phrase, the hearts within the bosoms. Everyone knows where hearts are. Commentators suggest the extra words are there for force: this is the real heart meant, the one inside you, not a figure of speech. So the verse isn't scolding anyone for poor eyesight. It describes an ordinary kind of blindness, the kind that comes from familiarity. The ruin you pass daily. The person you've stopped really looking at. The sky you haven't checked in weeks.
screen: `TRAVELERS WHO SAW THE RUINS.` · `NOT THE EYES THAT GO BLIND.` · `THE QALB: WHERE YOU UNDERSTAND.` · `BLINDNESS BY FAMILIARITY.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing in front of you that you see every day, a mug, your hand, the view from the window, and look at it as if you'd just arrived from very far away. Where did it come from, who made it, what has it been through? Let your eyes rest there until the understanding catches up; if you pray, you can ask for a seeing heart.
Blind hearts. In Surah Al-Hajj, it isn't the eyes that go blind, but the hearts within the chests: seeing without understanding. Today's word.
Your line: hearts see. Eyes can look for years before the heart takes it in. That's day four hundred eighty-seven.

488.title: Houses of worship protected
488.hook: permission to defend is given, for otherwise monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques would be pulled down (22:39–40)
488.howItsDone: Muslim scholars and community leaders often cite 22:40 when speaking about the protection of places of worship, including after attacks on churches, synagogues, temples and mosques.

segments.voice: Yesterday: blind hearts, seeing with the eyes but not understanding. Your line was hearts see.

In Mecca, the early Muslims were mocked, boycotted and harmed. Through all of it, they were told to be patient and not to strike back. Then they left their homes and went north to Medina. Around that time, according to commentators, came the first verses that gave permission to fight back. What's striking is the reason the verses give. It isn't only, you've been wronged. It's a list of buildings.
screen: `THE REASON IS A LIST OF BUILDINGS.`

segments.voice: Verse thirty-nine says permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged. Verse forty describes them: people driven from their homes unjustly, only because they said, our Lord is God. Then it explains why such permission exists at all. If God did not check some people by means of others, Pickthall says, "cloisters and churches and oratories and mosques, wherein the name of Allah is oft mentioned, would assuredly have been pulled down." Four kinds of building, in Arabic: sawami', biya', salawat, masajid. Commentators explain them roughly this way: sawami' are the retreats of monks and hermits; biya' are churches; salawat, in a common reading, are the prayer houses of the Jews; and masajid are mosques. The mosque comes last in the list. The phrase, where the name of God is often remembered, sits over all four; commentators differ on whether it belongs to the mosques alone or to every house in the list, and some take it the wider way. And this list sits in the very verse that first allows a persecuted community to defend itself. The reason given isn't only: protect your own. It's that without some check on oppression, places of prayer of every kind come down. History offers plenty of examples where that ideal was broken, by people of many faiths. The verse still stands as a measure. A defense that pulls down a church or a synagogue has forgotten the reason it was permitted in the first place.
screen: `DRIVEN OUT FOR SAYING: OUR LORD IS GOD.` · `CLOISTERS, CHURCHES, ORATORIES, MOSQUES.` · `THE MOSQUE COMES LAST IN THE LIST.` · `THE REASON IS THE MEASURE.`

segments.voice: Picture the places of worship near where you live, a mosque, a church, a synagogue, a temple, a gurdwara, a small room where people meet to pray, full of people on a Friday, a Saturday, a Sunday. If you pray, you can ask for their protection, all of them. If you don't, simply wish them safety.
Masajid. Mosques, named last in 22:40's list of houses of worship, cloisters, churches, oratories and mosques, protected together. Today's word.
Your line: all houses of prayer protected. The mosque is named last, beside the rest. Four hundred eighty-eight days now.

489.title: Humble in prayer
489.hook: successful are the believers who are humble in their prayer and turn from idle talk (23:1–3)
489.howItsDone: In the five daily prayers, Muslims are taught to pause at rest in each position, called tuma'nina, and teachers speak of khushu' as the inner stillness the outward rest is meant to support.

segments.voice: Yesterday: masajid, last in a list of houses of prayer protected together. Your line was all houses of prayer protected.

A man walks into the mosque in Medina, prays quickly, and comes over to greet the Prophet ﷺ. The Prophet returns his greeting and says: go back and pray, for you have not prayed. The man prays again the same way, and returns. Go back and pray; you have not prayed. A third time. Finally the man says: by the One who sent you with the truth, I don't know how to do it better. Teach me. Bukhari records what he was told. Today, a new surah, Al-Mu'minun, the Believers.

The surah opens with a promise. Pickthall: "Successful indeed are the believers who are humble in their prayers". Among the first things named next is turning away from idle talk. Humble in their prayers is khashi'un, people with khushu'. It's a hard word to put in English. The Qur'an uses the same root for land lying still and lowly, waiting for rain, and for voices gone hushed before God on the Last Day. So khushu' isn't only a feeling of humility. It's a stillness, a settling, where the noise goes down and attention gathers. The man in the mosque wasn't lazy or rude. He was going fast. And the Prophet's teaching to him, in Bukhari's account, was mostly about time. Bow until you are at rest in your bowing. Rise until you're standing straight. Prostrate until you are at rest in prostration. Sit until you're at rest sitting. At rest, again and again. Not more words, not harder feelings: slower bodies. That's why the next line of the surah fits: turning from idle talk. Khushu' is hard to reach with a phone buzzing in your pocket and half a conversation still running in your head. The hurried man got three chances and then a lesson, not a scolding. Khushu' isn't a test you pass once. It's a place you return to, one position at a time.
screen: `SUCCESSFUL ARE THE HUMBLE IN PRAYER.` · `KHUSHU': STILL, HUSHED, LOWLY.` · `BOW UNTIL YOU ARE AT REST.` · `TURN FROM IDLE TALK.`

segments.voice: If you pray, take the next prayer you're due to pray, and let every position come to rest before you move to the next. If you don't, do one ordinary thing that way right now: stand slowly, sit slowly, take one breath all the way to the end. Let each part finish before the next begins.
Khushu'. Humility in prayer, a stillness where attention gathers, like land lying quiet before rain. Today's word.
Your line: not more words, slower bodies. Stillness is a place to return to. Until tomorrow.

490.title: Clay, drop, clot, bone, flesh
490.hook: the stages of a human's making, then another creation (23:12–14)
490.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite 23:12–14 when reflecting on human creation, and the closing phrase 'fa tabarak Allahu ahsanu l-khaliqin' is said by some on seeing a newborn or something beautifully made.

segments.voice: Yesterday: khushu', stillness in prayer. Your line was not more words, slower bodies. Today closes the week.

Put two fingers on the inside of your wrist. Wait a second. There. That small, steady knock has been going since before you were born, and you didn't start it. Nobody asked whether you wanted a heartbeat, or bones, or the particular shape of your hands. Al-Mu'minun, just after describing the believers, tells how any human being is made, from the very beginning. It takes three verses, and it ends with a sentence of pure praise.

The verses move in steps, and each step has a word. First, a sulala min tin, an extract of clay, an essence drawn from the earth. Then a nutfa, a drop, placed in a safe lodging. Then the drop becomes an 'alaqa, a word Pickthall translates clot; its root carries the sense of something that clings. Then a mudgha, a little lump; the word means something chewed. Then bones, and the bones are clothed with flesh. Clay, drop, clot, bone, flesh. Then the turn. Pickthall: "and then produced it as another creation. So blessed be Allah, the Best of creators!" Another creation. After all the stages comes something that isn't just one more stage. Some commentators, citing reports from Ibn 'Abbas, read this as the moment the spirit is breathed in: the lump of tissue becomes someone. Some modern writers have compared these verses to modern embryology, and others caution against reading them as a science textbook. Either way, the verse doesn't end in a lab report. It ends in tabarak, blessed. Commentators tell a story that a companion, hearing these verses for the first time, said the closing praise aloud before it was recited, and was told that's exactly how it ends. It's a story people tell, and its chain is debated. But it shows how the passage feels: you climb the stages, and the praise is the natural top of the stairs.
screen: `AN EXTRACT OF CLAY, THEN A DROP.` · `CLOT, LUMP, BONE, FLESH.` · `THEN: ANOTHER CREATION.` · `BLESSED, THE BEST OF CREATORS.`

segments.voice: Put two fingers on your wrist or the side of your neck, count a few beats, then stop counting and just feel them. Think of the stages it took to get here: earth, a drop, a lump, bones, flesh, and then whatever it is that makes you you. If you pray, you can say the verse's ending: blessed is God, the best of creators.
Clay. Where the human story starts in this surah: an extract of clay, then drop, clot, lump, bone and flesh, then another creation. Today's word.
Your line: blessed is the best creator. Every stage ends in praise. That's the week.
